title: Taking a Matatu
culturalNote: Matatus are privately-owned minibuses that are the primary form of public transport in Nairobi. Routes are numbered but not always signed — locals know them. You pay the kondakta (conductor) in cash, and shout or gesture when you want to alight.

vocabulary.exampleContext: Said to the conductor when you're approaching your stop
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Kenyan speakers commonly use the 'Na-' shortform for first-person present where sanifu uses the full 'Nina-' prefix

vocabulary.exampleContext: The person who collects fares and calls out the route
vocabulary.sanifuNote: 'Kondakta' is a Kenyan borrowing from English 'conductor'; sanifu uses a descriptive phrase

vocabulary.exampleContext: 'Tao stage' means the town centre stop
vocabulary.sanifuNote: 'Stage' is a Kenyan English borrowing used universally; sanifu uses the formal Swahili term
Two deviations: the 'Na-' shortform for first-person present, plus 'tao' as Sheng for 'town' instead of the sanifu 'mjini'

vocabulary.exampleContext: Ask the conductor before or after boarding
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Both are understood; 'Bei ngapi?' is the faster, more common Kenyan form

vocabulary.exampleContext: Used urgently if the conductor misses your stop
Using the Nairobi neighbourhood nickname; conductors call routes by these names
vocabulary.sanifuNote: Same 'Na-' shortform; Kenyan speech also abbreviates neighbourhood names freely

vocabulary.exampleContext: Waved at a passing matatu to flag it down
vocabulary.sanifuNote: 'Beba' literally means 'carry'; Kenyans use it informally to flag matatus; sanifu uses the more formal imperative form

exchange.speaker: Abiria
exchange.english: I'm going to town, how much?

exchange.speaker: Abiria
exchange.english: I'm getting off here — the town stop.
